EPYC already has OpenCode integration, typed decisions, prepared-action validation, prefix caching, persistent REPL state, session fencing, EvalTower recovery, and belief adapters. REPL robustness: forward pickled_globals through two constructors that currently drop them; prevent reuse/checkpointing after an execution-thread timeout.

"Monty migration, SDM adoption, weight training and looped-model ports are no longer implementation campaigns. General research critiques constrain candidate-selection beliefs instead." - why were they deemed not relevant?

"I applied that requirement poorly. The original plan already acknowledged prepared-action validation, decision receipts, persistent REPL state and session fencing. Saying I subsequently “discovered” that infrastructure was misleading. The failure was allowing generic research concerns to justify new contracts and validators without demonstrating that EPYC lacked them or that they would improve an existing operational path.
I over-weighted “build reusable primitives” and under-weighted “identify the concrete project need first.”" - dispatch a subagent to investigate how to make this more robust in the future. I'm now worried that past research intake sessions have ignored crucially actionable work that should've been surfaced. Building reusable primitives isn't bad per se, but it MUST be contextualized among project objectives, otherwise we end up eating resources painting bike sheds so to speak.

"Monty — execution robustness. EPYC’s execution-thread timeout does not terminate the underlying computation. A disposable, resource-limited execution backend could address a problem that timeout poisoning alone cannot. Existing persistent CPython state weakens the startup-speed argument, but does not eliminate the isolation argument. The relevant question is whether Monty can support a specific EPYC workload and its callbacks—not whether to migrate the entire REPL.
SDM — routing quality and inference cost. It could challenge the existing routing classifier using the same decision-time features and eligible outcome-labelled cohort. Learning/promotion gates constrain deployment; they do not, by themselves, establish that a small offline comparison is inappropriate. I made the candidate posture too restrictive without establishing that distinction.
Multi-harness RL — tool-use efficiency and portability. Correctness-gated reductions in tool calls or tokens could benefit EPYC. The project also has actual language-model training machinery; it is not limited to router Q updates. What remains unestablished is the particular checkpoint, workload and training intervention worth testing—not the relevance of weight training itself.
Looped models — prefill latency. The relevant hypothesis is reducing prefill cost while retaining teacher decoding. That could matter to orchestration paths dominated by repeated long-context prefill. Compatibility and port effort remain unresolved, and the research does not establish an EPYC end-to-end benefit. Those are comparison prerequisites, not grounds for declaring the technique irrelevant." - what? There are tons of crucial insights here that should be integrated into our stack's functioning!
